notes.findings: COLD OPEN, to camera before the deck: Nebius just posted the wildest quarter on the Nasdaq and the stock jumped a third in a day. But its entire profit this year is a paper markup of a company it does not even control — and that is just the first of five things buried in the filings that never made the press release. THEN the slide: here are all five. Each one changes how you should read this company, and we will take them one at a time — watch the counter in the corner so you know where we are. TARGET 26s.
notes.quarter: First, the quarter as they reported it. Revenue five hundred eighty-two million, up four hundred fifty-four percent — that is not a typo. Adjusted EBITDA turned properly positive at a forty-one percent margin. But look at the bottom half: still an operating loss, still a net loss, and an interest bill that went from five million to a hundred and nineteen. And that half-year profit figure you will see quoted? That is finding number one: every dollar of it is a paper markup of their ClickHouse stake — a private database company whose funding round Nebius did not even join. Strip that out and the half year is a loss. TARGET 28s.
notes.leverage: Now the genuinely impressive part, and I want to give it its due. Each dot on this curve is one quarter, working left to right: revenue across the bottom, profit margin up the side. Two years ago this was a thirty-two million dollar quarter losing a dollar forty for every dollar it sold. Eight quarters later revenue is eighteen times bigger and the adjusted margin is plus forty-one. That is what real operating leverage looks like drawn on one line — the AI cloud business itself ran at a fifty percent margin this quarter. This part of the story is real. TARGET 26s.
notes.arrpath: Here is their run-rate revenue, the number this company guides on — and its history with promises. December 2024: ninety million, and their own release admits that was below guidance. Then they guided seven hundred fifty to a billion for the end of 2025, raised it in August, and delivered one point two five billion — a genuine beat. It is three billion now. But look at the last point: the 2026 guide is seven to nine billion. That means the run-rate has to more than double in six months. They have done it before — they are asking you to believe they do it again, on a number ten times bigger. TARGET 30s.
notes.rpo: Can they? Here is the case that they can: thirty-seven and a half billion dollars of signed contracts. Microsoft alone signed up to seventeen point four billion, with options to nineteen point four. Meta added about three billion. That bottom bar is everything Nebius sold in the last twelve months — the order book is nearly twenty-eight times that. But two footnotes. Only about a third of it turns into revenue in the next two years. And the company's own annual report says, in writing, that it has limited experience delivering long-term contracts like these. The mountain is real; so is the climb. TARGET 28s.
notes.cashwalk: Finding two, and it is the big one. Headline: four and a half billion dollars of operating cash flow in six months. Sounds like a money machine. Walk it: four point four billion of that is customer prepayments — money for compute they have not delivered yet, recognized over as much as five years. What the business generated by actually running is a hundred and nine million. Against eight point one billion of capital spending. This company is not self-funding — it is customer-funded and debt-funded. And on the debt: the first convertible bonds come due in twenty twenty-nine, and the newest ones repay a hundred and twenty cents on every dollar borrowed at maturity. The clock is real. TARGET 32s.
notes.refundable: And that prepaid money comes with strings. This is the company's own accounting note, word for word — including amounts that may be refundable. They never say how much. The balance is six billion dollars, which is seventy-four percent of all the cash you see on the balance sheet. And buried in the interest note: they pay interest on advances from major customers. Think about what that means — a prepayment you pay interest on is a loan wearing a different name. The cash pile is real, but most of it is other people's money with conditions attached. TARGET 28s.
notes.depreciation: The next finding is one sentence in the estimates note. In January, Nebius decided its servers last five years instead of four. Perfectly legal, arguably even reasonable. But apply the arithmetic: this single change cut this quarter's depreciation by forty-three million dollars — without it, the loss is two hundred twenty-four million, not one ninety. And the disclosed benefit only covers servers owned before 2026. The eight billion dollars of kit they bought this year gets the friendlier math too, and that benefit is not disclosed anywhere. The press release does not mention any of this. TARGET 26s.
notes.customers: Next finding: the customer list did not grow — it was replaced. A year ago customers A and B were more than half of all revenue. Today both have vanished from the disclosure table entirely, and three brand-new names — almost certainly Microsoft and Meta among them — carry fifty-nine percent. This is what it looks like when a company graduates from startups to hyperscalers, and that is genuinely good news. But understand the shape of the risk: three counterparties now decide this company's future, and twelve months ago none of them were here. TARGET 26s.
notes.insiders: The last finding — what the people inside are doing with their own money. Nebius insiders only started filing Form 4s in March. Since then: a hundred fifty-seven million dollars sold, across eight people — the founder, the CFO, the CTO, the chief revenue officer, the infrastructure chief. Purchases on the open market: zero. To be fair, about half the filings cite pre-arranged trading plans, and executives at four-x stocks always sell some. But the biggest single month of selling was May, right into the run-up — and nobody, at any price, bought. TARGET 26s.
notes.peers: So what are you paying? I have put everyone on the same honest yardstick — market value against the latest reported quarter annualized, growth beside it, because expensive and expensive-for-its-growth are different claims. CoreWeave, the closest pure comparison, costs about six dollars per dollar of current sales. Amazon and Oracle sit lower still. Nebius costs thirty-two. Yes, it is growing four times faster than CoreWeave — but you are paying nearly six times the price per sales dollar for that growth. TARGET 24s.
notes.street: One more thing before my call — what the analysts actually pencil in. Eight of them cover it. Their average price target is below where the stock trades after this jump. And their earnings estimates are the part nobody quotes: losses per share getting bigger every year through 2028, because depreciation and interest keep growing with the buildout. Thin coverage, so hold it loosely — but notice that not even the bulls put profits on paper this decade. TARGET 22s.
notes.call: So here is the whole story on one ruler. The bracket is my model: the left tick is the bear case, the middle of the shaded zone is my base case, and the right tick is a bull case that needs fifty percent compound growth for five straight years with margins they have never shown. Now look where today's price sits — past the top of the whole bracket. Everything genuinely great about this company — the growth, the contracts, the customers, all four chips under the chart — is already paid for at this price. So my call is WATCH, and my line is marked on the ruler: halfway between my base and bull cases. Near it or below, the odds flip toward you. If the stock hands back a chunk of this move while the contracts keep landing, that is when it gets interesting. That is the fundamentals — now let us see what the chart says. TARGET 32s.
